summary: Nehemiah returns from a stay at the Persian court and finds the covenant fraying on every front: Tobiah — the old enemy — has a storeroom inside the temple courts; the Levites have gone home unpaid; merchants are treading wine-presses and selling fish on the Sabbath; men have married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, and their children speak 'half in the language of Ashdod'; and the high priest's own grandson has married Sanaballat's daughter. Nehemiah cleans house — and prays 'Remember me, O our God, for good.'
whyItMatters: The book's last chapter is its most sobering: within years of signing the covenant, every major promise had bent. Nehemiah's reforms are forceful — furniture thrown out, gates shut, hair plucked — and his repeated prayer 'Remember me, O my God' leaves the reader to weigh both the zeal and the cost.

context.author: Nehemiah, first-person memoir
context.date: Nehemiah's second term as governor, after 433 BC (his 32nd year of Artaxerxes)
context.setting: Jerusalem — temple courts, city gates, and homes
context.literaryForm: First-person narrative of reforms, punctuated by short prayers

outline.heading: Aliens separated
outline.note: The law read: Ammonites and Moabites excluded — the Balaam history recalled

outline.heading: Tobiah evicted; the Levites restored
outline.note: The enemy housed in a temple storeroom; unpaid Levites recalled and the tithes reinstated

outline.heading: Sabbath commerce stopped
outline.note: Gates shut before Sabbath; merchants warned off the wall

outline.heading: Mixed marriages corrected
outline.note: Children speaking 'half in the language of Ashdod'; Solomon cited as the warning

outline.heading: The high priest's grandson expelled
outline.note: Son-in-law of Sanaballat — chased out; the priesthood purged

keyVerses.text: And I came to Jerusalem, and I understood the mischief which Eliasib had done in the case of Tobias, in making for him a treasury in the court of the house of God.
keyVerses.why: The scandal in one line: the man who mocked the wall now keeps an apartment in God's own courts — arranged by the high priest.

keyVerses.text: And I strove with the commanders, and said, Wherefore has the house of God been abandoned? and I assembled them, and set them in their place.
keyVerses.why: Unpaid Levites had fled to their fields — worship collapses quietly, by payroll, before it collapses loudly.

keyVerses.text: What is this evil thing which ye do, and profane the sabbath-day?
keyVerses.why: Nehemiah's question to the nobles — the Sabbath was the covenant's public sign, visible to every trading nation.

keyVerses.text: And the offering of the wood-bearers was at certain set times, and in the times of the first-fruits. Remember me, O our God, for good.
keyVerses.why: The book's final sentence — the same prayer as chapter 15, now covering a lifetime of costly reform.

questions.question: Why exclude Ammonites and Moabites specifically?
questions.answer: The law of Moses itself (Deuteronomy 23:3-5) barred them 'for ever' for refusing Israel bread and water on the exodus road and hiring Balaam to curse them — quoted here in verse 2. The assembly applies a standing statute when the mixed-marriage problem surfaces; it is law, not new prejudice.

questions.question: How did Tobiah — the enemy — get a room in the temple?
questions.answer: Family ties: the high priest Eliasib was 'connected with Tobias' (23:4-5), and chapter 16 showed nobles intermarried with his house. While Nehemiah was away at the Persian court, the alliance moved into the building itself. Reform undone by relationships is the oldest story in leadership.

questions.question: Why was Sabbath-keeping worth shutting the city gates for?
questions.answer: The Sabbath was Israel's covenant sign — the visible weekly statement that God, not the market, is Lord. Nehemiah warns that their fathers' Sabbath-breaking helped bring the exile (23:18). With traders camping outside the walls to catch Sabbath customers, the gates themselves became the enforcement.

questions.question: Was plucking out hair and striking them excessive?
questions.answer: It is corporal punishment, and readers have winced at it in every century. Context: Nehemiah 'contended, cursed, struck some, plucked their hair, and made them swear' — a governor enforcing a signed covenant whose violation threatened the community's survival. Whether the severity was right is a fair question; the text records it without flinching, and Nehemiah's own prayers show he knew his zeal would be weighed by God.

questions.question: Why expel the high priest's grandson instead of reforming him?
questions.answer: Because he had married Sanaballat's daughter — binding the priesthood to the man who spent twelve years trying to stop this very work. Nehemiah 'chased him away' (23:28) and prays for God to remember 'the defiling of the priesthood' (23:29). For a community whose whole identity was temple and covenant, the priesthood's integrity was not negotiable.

questions.question: What should I make of Nehemiah's repeated 'Remember me, O my God'?
questions.answer: It appears at least four times in the book (15:19, here in 23:14, 22, 31). He asks God — not history — to keep the record of his costly obedience. It is either the purest ambition or a subtle self-justification; the book leaves both readings open, which may be exactly why it ends there.

glossary.def: The high priest (Eliashib), who allied his family with Tobiah and Sanaballat.
A Philistine city; its language stood for the foreign speech replacing Hebrew among the children.
Artaxerxes I of Persia; his 32nd year is 433 BC.
Families assigned by lot to keep the altar supplied with wood (see chapter 20).
